messages.content:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Year

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, 'year' most commonly carries the symbolic sense of a complete, divinely appointed period of time — above all 'the acceptable year of the Lord,' i.e., the era of God's favor, salvation, and release. This draws on the Jubilee year (a fiftieth-year proclamation of liberty, debt release, and restoration) as a type of messianic redemption, which Jesus applies to his own ministry in the Nazareth synagogue. Thus 'year' symbolizes the full season or epoch of God's saving activity rather than a mere calendar unit.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 61:1-2 ('to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor')",
    "Luke 4:18-19 (Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and declares it fulfilled)",
    "Leviticus 25:8-13 (the Year of Jubilee: liberty, release, restoration)",
    "Isaiah 34:8 and 63:4 ('year of recompense' / 'year of my redeemed')",
    "Genesis 1:14 (heavenly lights appointed for 'seasons, days, and years' — time ordered by God)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The year-day principle in prophetic interpretation: a symbolic 'day' in prophecy stands for a literal year, so prophetic time periods (e.g., 70 weeks = 490 years; 1260 days = 1260 years) are decoded into years. Here 'year' functions as the unit of prophetic fulfillment. This was dominant in historicist Protestant interpretation and remains central in Seventh-day Adventist and some other traditions, though it is a minority view in contemporary mainstream scholarship.",
      "basis": [
        "Numbers 14:34 ('each day for a year')",
        "Ezekiel 4:5-6 ('a day for each year')",
        "Daniel 9:24-27 (the seventy 'weeks' understood as weeks of years)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A 'year' (or the 360-day prophetic year) as the building block of apocalyptic chronology: 'a time, times, and half a time' = three and a half years, equated with 42 months and 1260 days, symbolizing a limited, God-bounded period of tribulation or persecution.",
      "basis": [
        "Daniel 7:25; 12:7",
        "Revelation 11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Equivalence of vast divine time with human time — 'one day is as a thousand years' — used to argue that a 'year' or 'day' with God does not map onto human chronology, and in some schemes to support millennial or day-age readings.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 90:4",
        "2 Peter 3:8"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "'Year' as simply a complete natural cycle ordained by God, marking his faithfulness in the rhythm of seasons and the liturgical/festal calendar, without a distinct symbolic freight beyond ordered time under God's sovereignty.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 1:14; 8:22",
        "Exodus 23:14-17 (annual festal cycle)",
        "Psalm 65:11 ('you crown the year with your bounty')"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "Unlike terms such as 'lamb' or 'leaven,' 'year' does not have a single fixed symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation. The most recognizable symbolic usage is the 'year of the Lord's favor' (Jubilee/era of salvation), which is widely preached and cited, but much discussion of 'year' occurs within prophetic-chronology debates (year-day principle, prophetic 360-day year), where interpretive traditions diverge sharply (historicist vs. preterist vs. futurist vs. idealist). Any author claiming one settled symbolic meaning for 'year' is selecting from a genuinely contested field."
}

  "has_settled_consensus": true,

  "notes": "The symbolic meaning of 'year' often depends heavily on context. Soteriologically, it represents the era of Christ's grace (Jubilee). Eschatologically, it is frequently debated whether 'years' denote literal timeframes, symbolic epochs of completion, or apply a prophetic day-year calculus."
}

{
  "primary_meaning": "“Year” has no single settled biblical symbolic meaning. When used figuratively or typologically, its broadest conventional association is a complete or divinely appointed season—especially a time of favor, judgment, release, or restoration.",

    "Isaiah 61:1–2 and Luke 4:18–21 — “the year of the Lord’s favor” denotes the appointed era of salvation proclaimed and inaugurated by Christ.",

      ],

      ],

    },
    {
      "meaning": "In prophetic interpretation, one symbolic day represents one literal year—the “day-year principle.” This is especially prominent in historicist interpretation but is not accepted as a universal rule across Christian traditions.",
      "basis": [

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Christian interpretation does not generally treat “year” as carrying one fixed symbolic value. Its meaning is determined by context: most occurrences are literal, while symbolic uses variously concern an appointed season, Jubilee restoration, judgment, or particular prophetic calculations."
}

RESPONSE D
{
  "primary_meaning": "No single settled symbolic meaning; most often denotes a complete cycle of time or a designated period of divine action (favor, judgment, testing, or release), especially the 'acceptable/favorable year of the Lord' as the messianic era of salvation and grace",

      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },

      "meaning": "Application of the day-year principle in which observed days of sin or reconnaissance generate corresponding years of consequence (days symbolize years)",
      "basis": [
        "Numbers 14:34",
        "Ezekiel 4:5-6"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "Unlike more fixed biblical symbols (e.g., water, rock, lamb), 'year' functions mainly as a temporal measure whose symbolic force is context-dependent. The 'year of the Lord/favor' and Jubilee motifs are widely recognized in both Jewish and Christian teaching; the 360-day prophetic year and day-year principle are standard in historicist and some evangelical eschatology but secondary to the term itself. No single meaning dominates across the whole tradition."

BOOK ENTRY
A turning — shanah, written on the root to change, repeat, return: one complete cycle of time, at whatever scale the count is running — Jeremiah’s seventy “years” close only as seventy jubilees, and a thousand years pass as a day.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Jer 25:11-12; Dan 9:2, 24; Ps 90:4) · see Daniel Unsealed, ch. 36

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Jeremiah 25:11 — And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
Jeremiah 25:12 — And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the LORD, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations.
Daniel 9:2 — In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem.
Daniel 9:24 — Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.
Psalms 90:4 — For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
